title: Hypoalbuminaemia and Clinical Implications
subject: Medicine
summary: Low serum albumin reflects liver synthetic failure, protein loss or malnutrition and drives fluid shifts. Recognising causes, interpreting ascitic gradients and using albumin safely are key in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Serum albumin is the main plasma protein (55‑65% of total protein) with a molecular weight of 66 kDa. Hypoalbuminaemia is defined as <35 g/L (3.5 g/dL).
b: Measured by routine chemistry; no fasting required
Low value suggests reduced synthesis, loss, or dilution

sections.p: Clinical severity is graded by serum level and associated complications:
b: Mild: 30‑34 g/L – often asymptomatic
Moderate: 25‑29 g/L – peripheral oedema may appear
Severe: <25 g/L – ascites, pleural effusion, poor wound healing

sections.p: In East African hospitals the commonest drivers are:
b: Chronic liver disease (viral hepatitis B/C, alcohol, schistosomiasis) – reduced synthesis
Nephrotic syndrome (including malaria‑associated nephropathy) – urinary loss
Protein‑energy malnutrition – inadequate intake
Severe burns or extensive wounds – capillary leak
Heart failure on diuretics – dilutional low albumin; check SAAG >1.2 g/dL

sections.p: Low oncotic pressure leads to fluid accumulation and signs of poor nutrition.
b: Peripheral oedema, especially lower limbs
Ascites with shifting dullness
Pleural effusion, often right‑sided in cirrhosis
Fatigue, muscle wasting, delayed wound healing

t.b: Is the patient hypoalbuminaemic? – value <35 g/L confirms low oncotic pressure

t.a: Liver function tests (ALT, AST, bilirubin, INR)
t.b: Is the liver synthetic function impaired? – low albumin with raised INR suggests cirrhosis
Is there renal loss? – ≥3+ protein or >3 g/24 h points to nephrotic syndrome
Is ascites portal‑hypertensive? – SAAG >1.2 g/dL indicates portal pressure (e.g., cirrhosis, heart failure)

t.a: Full blood count and HIV test
t.b: Are there co‑existing infections or marrow suppression? – anemia, lymphopenia may guide further work‑up
Is heart failure contributing? – reduced EF or right‑sided pressures explain dilutional hypoalbuminaemia

sections.p: Severe hypoalbuminaemia predisposes to life‑threatening fluid shifts and infection.
b: Rapidly expanding ascites or pleural effusion causing respiratory distress
Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) – fever, abdominal pain, altered mental status
Severe oedema compromising circulation
Bleeding tendency due to low clotting factor synthesis

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first; albumin infusion is adjunctive.
b: Liver disease: antiviral therapy for hepatitis, abstinence from alcohol, treat schistosomiasis, consider diuretics with caution
Nephrotic syndrome: ACE‑inhibitor or ARB, salt restriction, treat underlying infection (e.g., malaria)
Malnutrition: high‑protein diet, oral supplements; in severe cases, therapeutic feeding programmes
Acute decompensation (SBP, large ascites): give 1 g/kg 20 % albumin over 2 h (if available) plus antibiotics for SBP
When albumin is unavailable: optimise diuretics, limit further fluid loss, use low‑sodium diet

sections.p: Monitor albumin weekly in acute settings, then monthly once stable.
b: Repeat serum albumin and LFTs after 2‑4 weeks of therapy
Educate patients on protein‑rich diet (legumes, eggs, dairy) and safe water
Vaccinate against hepatitis B, treat schistosomiasis, control malaria

sections.p: Conditions that also cause oedema but have different pathophysiology.
b: Hypo‑globulinaemia – low immunoglobulins, not oncotic pressure
Congestive heart failure – high‑pressure hydrostatic oedema, SAAG >1.2 g/dL but normal albumin
Dehydration can falsely raise albumin – assess clinical volume status
Hemolysis in the sample may lower measured albumin
SAAG requires accurate paired fluid and serum samples; mismatched timing skews gradient

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden respiratory compromise from massive pleural effusion
Signs of SBP: fever, abdominal pain, altered mental status

faq.q: Why is albumin given in spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
faq.a: It expands plasma volume, improves renal perfusion and reduces mortality when combined with antibiotics.

faq.q: Can low albumin occur with normal liver tests?
faq.a: Yes, in nephrotic syndrome, severe malnutrition or protein‑losing enteropathy.

faq.q: What does a SAAG >1.2 g/dL tell me?
faq.a: The ascites is due to portal hypertension (e.g., cirrhosis, heart failure) rather than peritoneal infection or malignancy.

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with chronic hepatitis B presents with new abdominal distension – what investigations clarify the cause of his ascites? — Order serum albumin, ascitic fluid albumin for SAAG, LFTs, and ultrasound; SAAG >1.2 g/dL points to portal hypertension.

A child with severe malaria develops peripheral oedema; serum albumin is 28 g/L. What is the primary mechanism? — Malaria‑induced capillary leak and renal protein loss; treat malaria and consider albumin if shock develops.

A patient on high‑dose furosemide for heart failure has serum albumin 32 g/L and new pleural effusion. How do you differentiate dilutional hypoalbuminaemia from true hepatic failure? — Check SAAG; >1.2 g/dL suggests portal hypertension, while low SAAG with normal liver enzymes points to diuretic‑induced dilution.

Why is albumin infusion avoided in patients with isolated nephrotic syndrome without hypovolemia? — It does not correct urinary protein loss and may worsen edema; focus on diuretics and ACE‑inhibitors.

During a ward round you see a patient with ascites, low albumin, and normal INR. What red flag prompts immediate antibiotics? — Development of fever, abdominal pain or altered mental status suggesting spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
Explain how hypoalbuminaemia contributes to wound dehiscence after surgery. — Low oncotic pressure impairs tissue turgor and protein delivery for collagen synthesis, delaying healing.
A pregnant woman in a low‑resource clinic has serum albumin 34 g/L. Should you give albumin? — No, unless she shows signs of hypovolemia or severe pre‑eclampsia; focus on nutritional support.
How does chronic schistosomiasis lead to low albumin? — Repeated hepatic fibrosis reduces synthetic function; treat with praziquantel and monitor liver function.
